title: The Leader Who Cannot Delegate
subtitle: A pastoral guide to delegation in church leadership, why the indispensable leader is a liability, and how to hand off real authority so the ministry can grow past you.

sections.title: The Man Without Whom Nothing Happens
sections.body:
Every church has felt it, the leader who has to touch everything. He approves the bulletin, signs off on the small group curriculum, returns every email himself, and is genuinely proud of how hard he works. The staff cannot move without him. The volunteers wait on his word. And he tells himself this is excellence, when it is actually a cage he built and then locked himself inside.

The indispensable man is not a strong leader. He is a bottleneck wearing the costume of one. Everything that flows through him also stops at him, and so the whole ministry moves at exactly the speed of one exhausted person. He cannot take a vacation without things grinding to a halt, cannot get sick without a crisis, cannot die without the work dying with him. He has confused being central with being effective, and they are opposites.

Not strength. Fear in a strong man's clothes. Underneath the heroic workload is almost always something unflattering, a need to be needed, a distrust of everyone else, a suspicion that no one can do it as well as he can. Sometimes that suspicion is even true, and it does not matter, because a ministry that depends on one man's competence is a ministry one man tall, and God did not call you to build something that small.

sections.title: Why We Will Not Let Go
sections.body:
We all say we want to delegate. We attend the seminars, read the books, nod at the principle, and then we go back to doing everything ourselves. The gap between what we believe about delegation and what we actually do is enormous, and the reasons we will not let go are worth dragging into the light, because they are usually about us.

We will not delegate because we are afraid it will be done badly, and a thing done badly will reflect on us. We will not delegate because being needed feels like being valued, and handing off the work feels like handing off our worth. We will not delegate because it is faster to do it ourselves today, and we never count the cost of doing it ourselves every day forever. And underneath all of it, often, we will not delegate because we do not actually trust the people God has given us, and we have dressed our control up as conscientiousness.

I know every one of these from the inside. I have kept tasks I should have given away and told myself it was stewardship when it was fear. The hardest truth about delegation is that the obstacle is not the people who might fail you. The obstacle is your own grip, and your own grip is harder to pry loose than any external problem, because you do not experience it as a problem. You experience it as virtue.

sections.title: Hand Off the Authority, Not Just the Work
sections.body:
Most attempts at delegation fail because the leader gives away the task while keeping the authority, and a person responsible for an outcome they have no power to shape will be frustrated, then resentful, then gone. Real delegation transfers both, and that is exactly the part that costs the leader something.

Jethro told Moses, who was killing himself judging every dispute in Israel, to appoint capable men and give them real jurisdiction, deciding the small matters themselves and bringing only the great ones to him. Notice that Jethro did not tell Moses to get help with his caseload. He told Moses to give the cases away, to let other men decide, to release the authority and not just the labor. That is the model. Hand someone a whole responsibility and the freedom to make real decisions about it, including ones you would have made differently, and then live with the difference.

The old four-step pattern still works because it is honest about how people learn. You do it while they watch. You do it while they help. They do it while you help. They do it while you watch. Most leaders camp permanently at the second step, doing the work while letting people assist, and call the eternal assistant a leader in training. Push through to the fourth step, where they own it and you have stepped back, and where the work no longer waits on you because you finally let it go.

sections.title: The Mistakes You Prevent Are the Lessons You Steal
sections.body:
The hardest part of delegation is not the handoff. It is what comes after, when the person you delegated to does it differently than you would have, and sometimes does it worse, and you have to sit on your hands and let it happen. A leader who cannot tolerate that has not delegated anything. He has loaned out a task he intends to take back the moment it gets interesting.

People grow through ownership, and ownership includes the freedom to fail in survivable ways. The greeter who does it awkwardly the first month, the small group leader who handles a hard conversation clumsily, the staff member who makes a call you would not have made, these are not problems to be prevented. They are how leaders are made. If you swoop in and correct every decision, redo every imperfect effort, hover over every choice, you will produce dependents, not leaders, and the moment you step away the whole thing will fall, because it was never theirs.

This requires you to absorb some cost. Things will be done in ways you would not have chosen, and the church will survive it, and the people will grow because of it. The leader who needs everything done his way has not built a team. He has built an audience for his own competence. Let people own the work, including the part where they sometimes get it wrong, because the alternative is a ministry where only one person ever learns anything, and that ceiling is you.

sections.title: He Gave Gifts to Each One
sections.body:
When Jesus told the parable of the talents, the master did a striking thing. He went away. He handed his property to his servants, gave them real responsibility and real freedom, and left, and the whole point of the story is what they did when he was not standing over them. The servant the master praised was not the one who guarded the master's presence. It was the one who took what he was given and multiplied it on his own.

The leader who will not delegate has, in a sense, refused to let his people be those servants. He keeps everything in his own hands, buries the gifts of the people around him by never letting them be used, and then wonders why his church is full of spectators. He has made himself the only servant in the parable, and he is exhausted, and the ministry is exactly as large as one tired man, and it will end when he ends.

I have lived as that man, and I am still tempted back into him. The grip feels like faithfulness. It is actually a refusal to trust God with the people God provided. The leader who delegates is confessing something true, that the work is bigger than him, that the Spirit gifted others too, that he is a steward and not the owner. Do yourself out of a job. Multiply your life into people who can carry it without you. Because the goal was never to be indispensable. The goal was a harvest, and there is no harvest from a seed that will not leave your hand.
